lead: An amplifier cannot give high gain over a wide band of frequencies. In a single-pole amplifier the gain falls at 20 dB per decade above its dominant pole, so gain multiplied by bandwidth stays fixed. That constant is the gain-bandwidth product, GBW. The frequency where the open-loop gain falls to 1 is the transition frequency fT, and for a single-pole amplifier fT = GBW. Datasheets quote fT, and a designer uses it to find the closed-loop bandwidth at any gain: bandwidth = fT ÷ closed-loop gain.
prereq: You need: the upper cut-off frequency and the 0.707 point from Chapter 3.2, and the ideal op-amp model from Unit 6.

sections.h3: The gain falls, the product stays

blocks.text: Every amplifier has internal capacitance, so its gain falls at high frequency. In a single-pole amplifier one pole dominates: the gain is flat at A₀ up to the pole frequency f_p, and above f_p it falls at 20 dB per decade. A fall of 20 dB per decade means the gain halves every time the frequency doubles.

blocks.where: A(f) is the open-loop gain magnitude at frequency f, in V/V; A₀ is the low-frequency gain in V/V; f_p is the dominant pole frequency in Hz, the point where A = 0.707 A₀; f is the signal frequency in Hz.

blocks.text: When f is much larger than f_p, the 1 under the square root can be dropped, and the gain becomes A(f) ≈ A₀ f_p / f. Multiply both sides by f: A(f) × f ≈ A₀ f_p. The product is a constant, independent of frequency. That constant is the gain-bandwidth product, written GBW = A₀ × f_p, measured in hertz.

The product stays fixed because the slope is fixed. Every extra unit of gain costs the same factor of bandwidth, so you can trade one for the other but cannot get both. An op-amp with A₀ = 2×10⁵ and f_p = 10 Hz has GBW = 2 MHz; its gain is about 200 at 10 kHz and about 20 at 100 kHz.

Put A(f) = 1 in the falling part of the curve: 1 = A₀ f_p / f_T, so f_T = A₀ × f_p = GBW. At f_T the open-loop gain is exactly 1 (0 dB). A signal passed through the bare op-amp comes out with the same amplitude it went in; above f_T the op-amp attenuates.

f_T is the same number as GBW, written as a frequency. Some syllabi call it the unity-gain frequency, unity-gain bandwidth, or the cut-off frequency. A datasheet may print "gain bandwidth product 2 MHz" or "unity gain bandwidth 2 MHz". Keep it separate from f_p: f_p is the −3 dB point of the open-loop curve, f_T is the 0 dB point.

Engineers treat f_T as the figure of merit for speed. Two op-amps with the same low-frequency gain can differ tenfold in f_T, and the faster one gives ten times the closed-loop bandwidth at every gain.

blocks.where: A_CL is the closed-loop gain of the non-inverting amplifier in V/V; R_f is the feedback resistor in Ω; R_1 is the resistor from the inverting input to ground in Ω.

blocks.text: Negative feedback pushes the closed-loop pole up by the same factor that it pushes the gain down. The closed-loop response is still single-pole, with bandwidth BW_CL = f_T / A_CL. The gain-bandwidth product of the closed-loop amplifier is A_CL × BW_CL = f_T, unchanged from the open-loop value. See Unit 4, Feedback Amplifiers and Oscillators, for the full derivation.

At f_T = 2 MHz, a gain of 20 gives 100 kHz and a gain of 200 gives 10 kHz. A voltage follower, A_CL = 1, gives the full 2 MHz and is the fastest configuration. A closed-loop gain set lower than 1 is not possible without extra circuitry, so f_T is the ceiling for closed-loop bandwidth.

For the inverting amplifier, the bandwidth is set by the noise gain 1 + R_f/R_1, not by the signal gain R_f/R_1. A gain-of-10 inverting stage behaves like a non-inverting stage of gain 11 for bandwidth.

One forward pointer: at large signal amplitudes the output cannot move faster than the slew rate, so the usable full-power bandwidth is lower than f_T/A_CL even in a single-pole part. That limit, and its link to f_T, is covered in Unit 5.

figure.caption: Open-loop gain of a single-pole op-amp with f_T = 2 MHz. The curve meets the unity-gain line at 2 MHz, and at 10 Hz it is still at 2×10⁵, the low-frequency gain A₀.

spec.aria: A log-log plot of open-loop gain against frequency. The gain falls as 1/f and reaches 1 at 2 MHz, so the gain-bandwidth product is 2×10⁶ Hz.

examples.question: A single-pole op-amp has a low-frequency open-loop gain A₀ = 200,000 and a transition frequency f_T = 2 MHz. (a) Find the dominant pole frequency f_p. (b) State the gain-bandwidth product. (c) Find the closed-loop bandwidth when the op-amp is used in a non-inverting amplifier of gain 20.
steps: For a single-pole amplifier GBW = f_T = A₀ × f_p, so f_p = f_T / A₀.
GBW = f_T = 2 MHz = 2×10⁶ Hz. Check: A₀ × f_p = 2×10⁵ × 10 Hz = 2×10⁶ Hz.
The closed-loop gain is A_CL = 20, so BW_CL = f_T / A_CL.
Check the meaning: at 100 kHz the open-loop gain is f_T/f = 2×10⁶/1×10⁵ = 20, exactly the closed-loop gain. The loop gain has fallen to 1 there, which is where the closed-loop response is 3 dB down.
examples.answer: f_p = 10 Hz, GBW = 2 MHz, and the closed-loop bandwidth at gain 20 is 100 kHz.
examples.check:
A0 = 200_000
fT = 2e6
fp = fT / A0
gbw = A0 * fp
bw = fT / 20
print(int(fp))
print(int(gbw))
print(int(bw))

traps: Using f_T as the closed-loop bandwidth at every gain. The bandwidth is f_T divided by the closed-loop gain: at gain 20 it is 100 kHz, not 2 MHz.
Mixing up f_p and f_T. f_p is the open-loop −3 dB point, where gain is 0.707 A₀; f_T is the 0 dB point, where gain is 1. They are linked by f_T = A₀ × f_p.
Applying gain × bandwidth = f_T when a second pole sits near the working frequency. The product then falls, and the simple formula overestimates the real bandwidth.
Feeding a pole in rad/s into a formula that expects hertz. If ω_p = 62.8 rad/s is given, convert first: f_p = ω_p/2π = 10 Hz.
For an inverting amplifier, putting the signal gain R_f/R_1 into f_T/A_CL. Use the noise gain 1 + R_f/R_1 instead.

quiz.q: Define the transition frequency of an amplifier.
quiz.a: The frequency at which the open-loop gain magnitude falls to 1 (0 dB). For a single-pole amplifier f_T = A₀ × f_p.

quiz.q: Write the gain-bandwidth product relation for a single-pole amplifier and name each term with its unit.
quiz.a: GBW = A₀ × f_p = f_T, where A₀ is the low-frequency gain (V/V), f_p is the dominant pole (Hz), and GBW and f_T are in Hz.

quiz.q: Why does the product of gain and bandwidth stay constant above f_p?
quiz.a: Above f_p the gain falls at a fixed 20 dB per decade, so A(f) ≈ A₀f_p/f. Multiplying by f gives the constant A₀f_p. Doubling the gain halves the bandwidth, so the product cannot change.

quiz.q: A single-pole amplifier has A₀ = 100,000 and f_p = 20 Hz. Find f_T and the closed-loop bandwidth at a gain of 50.
An op-amp has f_T = 4 MHz. Find the closed-loop bandwidth at a gain of 25, and the bandwidth of the same op-amp as a voltage follower.
quiz.a: At gain 25: BW = 4×10⁶/25 = 160 kHz. As a voltage follower A_CL = 1, so BW = 4×10⁶/1 = 4 MHz.

quiz.q: A student measures closed-loop bandwidth 90 kHz at gain 10 and 12 kHz at gain 100 on the same op-amp. Is the amplifier single-pole over this range? What does the answer mean for quoting one f_T?
quiz.a: The products are 900 kHz and 1.2 MHz, which are not equal, so the single-pole model fails and a second pole is bending the curve. A single f_T is only a rough guide here; the designer must check the datasheet gain-frequency curve near the working gain.

quiz.q: Two op-amps have the same f_T = 1 MHz but low-frequency gains of 10⁵ and 10⁶. Compare their closed-loop bandwidths at a gain of 100. What does this show about f_T as a figure of merit?
quiz.a: Both give BW = 10⁶/100 = 10 kHz. The bandwidth at a fixed closed-loop gain depends only on f_T, not on A₀. A₀ fixes the pole instead: f_p = f_T/A₀ = 10 Hz and 1 Hz respectively. So f_T is the single number that compares speed.

beyond: Not for the exam. Datasheets lead with f_T because it sets the fastest signal a given closed-loop gain can pass; the classic 741 sits near 1 MHz while modern CMOS op-amps reach hundreds of MHz. For a bipolar transistor the same symbol f_T means something narrower: the frequency where the short-circuit current gain h_fe falls to 1, and radio-frequency devices are also graded by f_max, where power gain reaches 1. The slew-rate limit closes the loop, because a sine of frequency f and peak amplitude V_p needs a rate of 2π f V_p, so f_T alone does not guarantee a clean large-signal output; see Unit 5. Search 'unity gain bandwidth op amp', 'transition frequency bipolar transistor' and 'full-power bandwidth'.
